title: Credibility Booster: Sharing Bits o' Pedagogy
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart uses a recent pop-up debate on the 'scramble for Africa' to illustrate a low-lift credibility tactic: briefly narrating the pedagogical reasoning behind a lesson sequence to students after the fact. He walks through the knowledge-building steps that preceded the debate (notes, primary sources, memorized dates, direct explanation) to show these individual activities cohere into a single repeated instructional pattern from his book These 6 Things. The heart of the piece is the short debrief he actually gave students, explaining why pop-up debates function as a form of self-quizzing that consolidates prior learning. He closes by connecting the practice to his Care-Competence-Passion (CCP) credibility framework, arguing that naming your pedagogical why signals all three at once.
points: Briefly explaining the 'why' behind a lesson move to students functions as a credibility signal, not just a transparency courtesy — it hits Care, Competence, and Passion simultaneously.
Stuart frames pop-up debates explicitly as a form of self-quizzing, tying an engagement activity back to retrieval-practice reasoning rather than presenting it as mere participation.
The tactic requires almost no extra planning: it's a 30-second verbal debrief appended to an activity already happening, making it a genuinely low-stress addition to a teacher's routine.

Individual activities (notes, primary sources, memorization, direct explanation) only build credibility as a coherent system when the teacher periodically names how they connect — otherwise students may experience them as disjointed tasks.
quotes: Once in a while, it's smart to tell your students a bit of the thinking behind your lessons. Let me give a recent example from my practice and then close by explaining what I think things like this do for credibility.

Now that might all sound complicated, but it's really just These 6 Things — lots of knowledge-building, reading, writing, and speaking/listening, on repeat all year long. When you give yourself years of deliberate practice in these few core areas of pedagogy, you end up internalizing them and creating coherent learning experiences.
One reason we do pop-up debates is because they're a great way to solidify our hold on the information we've been learning. It's a form of self-quizzing, which we've talked about lots before.
Do I care about you as students? You bet! Do I know a thing or two about teaching? I sure do! Is there a fire behind my planning — an urgency to see you grow in mastery?
So tomorrow, maybe tell your students a bit of your pedagogical why when you're together. It's a signal worth sending.
